minor_characters.name: Conky Daniels
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A notorious Boston Common 'blackguard' who looms in a schoolboy snowball fight as a figure of neighborhood legend (Ch 007).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He appears only in a single childhood street-fight anecdote and has no bearing on Adams's development or the book's central themes.

minor_characters.name: Dr. Parkman and P. P. F. Degrand
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Elderly friends dozing by John Quincy Adams’s sickbed in Mount Vernon Street, glimpsed during the grandfather’s final illness (Ch 004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: They are passing names in a family-scene vignette and add no thread to Adams’s long arc or thought.

minor_characters.name: The Irish Gardener
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A nameless Quincy gardener who jokes that the boy will be President, in a single childhood memory (Ch 004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: His one-line quip provides color but no consequence for plot, ideas, or recurring relationships.

minor_characters.name: Prince Caracciolo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The charming Neapolitan officer who commands the flea-ridden transport taking Adams to Garibaldi’s Palermo (Ch 011).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is a travel-stage cameo in the Garibaldi episode and never recurs or shapes Adams’s education.

minor_characters.name: Robert Browning
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Briefly encountered at Rome; Adams recalls Browning’s shock at seeing the guillotine and his talk of French cruelty (Ch 011).
minor_characters.reason_removable: The cameo is a one-off literary flourish that does not affect Adams’s choices or later reflections.

minor_characters.name: Sir Henry Holland
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A sociable London physician who hosts breakfasts and gives Adams a front-row tourist vantage on society (Ch 015).
minor_characters.reason_removable: His role is limited to facilitating introductions; cutting him does not change the London-learning throughlines.

minor_characters.name: Reynolds Hitt
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A friend in Paris whose Avenue du Bois attic Adams borrows in 1898–99 (Ch 023).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is an incidental landlord-ally with no thematic weight.

minor_characters.name: Raphael Pumpelly
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Geologist whose passing recommendation of Karl Pearson’s Grammar of Science helps send Adams down a reading path (Ch 031).
minor_characters.reason_removable: The intellectual turn can be preserved without naming the recommender; the book and ideas carry the weight.

minor_characters.name: Michael Herbert
minor_characters.appearances_summary: British ambassador who, with his wife, eases Hay’s Washington burdens (Ch 028).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He offers social smoothing in late chapters but is not needed to follow Hay’s diplomacy or Adams’s theory-making.

minor_characters.name: Mr. de Plehve
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Named in a terse street notice of his assassination that sends Adams into St. Pantaleon at Troyes (Ch 029).
minor_characters.reason_removable: The Russian interior minister’s death is an incidental trigger for a church visit; it does not alter the dynamic/virgin argument.

subplots.name: The Boston Common snowball war
subplots.reason_removable: The raucous boyhood melee (with heroes Savage and Marvin) is an entertaining set-piece but inessential to Adams’s later education, politics, or theory.

subplots.name: Garibaldi mission and Palermo interview
subplots.reason_removable: The brief field-report to Captain Palmer and a five‑minute look at Garibaldi provide travel color without shaping Adams’s subsequent diplomatic, historical, or scientific quests.

subplots.name: Fryston house party with Swinburne, Oliphant, and Stirling
subplots.reason_removable: This sparkling salon weekend displays literary society but its portraits do not advance Adams’s London learning or later hypotheses.

subplots.name: Authors’ Fund dinner and Swinburne encounters
subplots.reason_removable: The toasts and talk are witty tableaux that repeat the social-point already made, and can be summarized or cut without loss.

subplots.name: Browning’s guillotine shock in Rome
subplots.reason_removable: The anecdote underscores European moral paradoxes already covered in the Roman chapters; it can be dropped without changing the arc from Rome to Washington.

subplots.name: Learning to ride the bicycle at sixty
subplots.reason_removable: This late-life vignette of self-mockery adds charm, not structure, and can be omitted without affecting Adams’s leap to the Dynamo and Virgin.

subplots.name: St. Louis Exposition detour with the Hays
subplots.reason_removable: The 1904 trip reprises World’s‑Fair spectacle after Chicago and Paris and does not add to the Virgin‑and‑Dynamo or acceleration throughline.

subplots.name: Sir Henry Holland breakfasts and London introductions
subplots.reason_removable: This thread simply ferries Adams through clubs and callers; the social-intelligence he gains is captured elsewhere in fewer strokes.

digressions.topic: Bookish detours on Wordsworth, desultory reading, and lists of eighteenth‑century poets
digressions.reason_removable: These catalogues of tastes and book-chatter slow the Boston–Harvard thread without changing Adams’s verdict on formal schooling.

digressions.topic: Street‑level Boston lore and blackguard taxonomy
digressions.reason_removable: Extended neighborhood sociology (e.g., North‑enders and South‑enders) is local color that can be compressed without loss to the plot or themes.

digressions.topic: Long satire of Harvard manners and clubland social calibration
digressions.reason_removable: The essayistic roast of Cambridge sociability adds little to the intellectual plot once Adams has located the limits of college education.

digressions.topic: Salon‑by‑salon tours of Paris artists and expatriate chatter before 1900
digressions.reason_removable: The thumbnail tours repeat earlier social diagnostics and can be tightened to keep focus on the Virgin‑and‑Dynamo turn.
